# Mixed Models with an Extra Zero Part

`MixedModel` in **glmmadaptive** can also be used to fit zero-inflated and
two-part mixed effects models.  For both types of models, a suitable `family`
object must be specified, and the arguments `zi_fixed` and `zi_random` of
`MixedModel` come into play.  In these arguments the user specifies the fixed-
and random-effects formulas of the logistic regression for the zero-part of the
distribution.  Setting `zi_random=None` (the default) fits a zero-part with
only fixed effects and no random effects.

## Status of Python implementations

| Family (R) | Python class | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `zi.poisson()` | `ZIPoisson` | **Implemented** |
| `zi.negative.binomial()` | `ZINegativeBinomial` | **Implemented** |
| `hurdle.lognormal()` | `HurdleLogNormal` | Stub — not yet implemented |
| `hurdle.poisson()` | `HurdlePoisson` | Stub — not yet implemented |
| `hurdle.negative.binomial()` | `HurdleNegativeBinomial` | Stub — not yet implemented |

The two implemented families are demonstrated below with full Python code.
Sections covering the hurdle families include the R equivalents and a note
explaining that Python support will be added in a future release.

## Zero-Inflated Poisson Mixed Effects Model

We start by showing how to fit a zero-inflated Poisson (ZIP) mixed effects
model.  First, we simulate longitudinal data from a zero-inflated negative
binomial distribution:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.special import expit          # equivalent to R's plogis()
from scipy.stats import nbinom as sp_nbinom

from glmmadaptive import MixedModel
from glmmadaptive.families import ZIPoisson, ZINegativeBinomial
from glmmadaptive.results import MixModResults

np.random.seed(1234)
n = 100   # number of subjects
K = 8     # number of measurements per subject
t_max = 5 # maximum follow-up time

# Construct a DataFrame with the design:
# everyone has a baseline measurement, then measurements at random follow-up times
ids = np.repeat(np.arange(1, n + 1), K)
times = np.concatenate([
    np.concatenate([[0], np.sort(np.random.uniform(0, t_max, K - 1))])
    for _ in range(n)
])
sex_labels = np.repeat(["male"] * (n // 2) + ["female"] * (n // 2), K)

DF = pd.DataFrame({"id": ids, "time": times, "sex": sex_labels})
DF["sex_female"] = (DF["sex"] == "female").astype(float)

# Design matrices for the fixed and random effects — non-zero part
# Equivalent to model.matrix(~ sex * time) with 'female' as the non-reference level
X = np.column_stack([
    np.ones(n * K),
    DF["sex_female"],
    DF["time"],
    DF["sex_female"] * DF["time"],
])
Z = np.ones((n * K, 1))  # random intercept only

# Design matrices for the zero part  (~ sex)
X_zi = np.column_stack([np.ones(n * K), DF["sex_female"]])
Z_zi = np.ones((n * K, 1))  # random intercept for zero part

betas  = np.array([1.5, 0.05, 0.05, -0.03])  # fixed effects — non-zero part
shape  = 2.0                                   # NB size parameter
gammas = np.array([-1.5, 0.5])                # fixed effects — zero part
D11    = 0.5   # variance of random intercepts (non-zero part)
D22    = 0.4   # variance of random intercepts (zero part)

# Simulate correlated random effects
b = np.column_stack([
    np.random.normal(0, np.sqrt(D11), n),
    np.random.normal(0, np.sqrt(D22), n),
])

# Linear predictors
id_idx = DF["id"].values - 1
eta_y  = X @ betas  + (Z  * b[id_idx, :1]).sum(axis=1)
eta_zi = X_zi @ gammas + (Z_zi * b[id_idx, 1:2]).sum(axis=1)

# Simulate negative binomial counts (scipy uses p = size/(size + mu))
mu_y = np.exp(eta_y)
p_nb = shape / (shape + mu_y)
DF["y"] = sp_nbinom.rvs(n=shape, p=p_nb, random_state=1234)

# Introduce structural zeros
zi_mask = np.random.binomial(1, expit(eta_zi)).astype(bool)
DF.loc[zi_mask, "y"] = 0

print(f"Proportion of zeros: {(DF['y'] == 0).mean():.3f}")
DF.head(10)
```

A zero-inflated Poisson mixed model with only fixed effects in the zero part is
fitted with the following call to `MixedModel`.  The only changes from the
standard Poisson model are `family=ZIPoisson()` and the extra `zi_fixed`
argument:

```{python}
fm1 = MixedModel(
    fixed="y ~ sex * time",
    random="~ 1 | id",
    family=ZIPoisson(),
    data=DF,
    zi_fixed="~ sex",
).fit()

print(fm1.summary())
```

As in the R package, only the log link is available for the non-zero part and
the logit link for the zero part.  The estimated fixed effects for the two parts
are interpreted accordingly.

We extend `fm1` by allowing also for random intercepts in the zero part.  By
default the random intercept of the non-zero part and the random intercept of
the zero part are **correlated** (full covariance matrix $D$):

```{python}
fm2 = MixedModel(
    fixed="y ~ sex * time",
    random="~ 1 | id",
    family=ZIPoisson(),
    data=DF,
    zi_fixed="~ sex",
    zi_random="~ 1 | id",
).fit()

print(fm2.summary())
```

We test whether we need the extra random effect in the zero part using a
likelihood ratio test:

```{python}
print(MixModResults.anova(fm1, fm2))
```

The results suggest that the extra random effect improves the fit of the model.

## Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial Mixed Effects Model

We continue with the same data, but now account for the potential
over-dispersion using a zero-inflated negative binomial model.  The only
difference in the call is the `family` argument:

```{python}
gm1 = MixedModel(
    fixed="y ~ sex * time",
    random="~ 1 | id",
    family=ZINegativeBinomial(),
    data=DF,
    zi_fixed="~ sex",
).fit()

print(gm1.summary())
```

Because the data were actually generated from a negative binomial distribution,
`gm1` (ZINB) and `fm2` (ZIP with ZI random effect) are **non-nested**.  We can
still compare them via information criteria by calling `anova()` without a
formal LRT:

```{python}
# Non-nested comparison: display AIC / BIC without a p-value
res = MixModResults.anova(gm1, fm2)
print(res)
```

Accounting for over-dispersion tends to improve the fit more than including the
extra random intercept in the zero part.

## Two-Part Mixed Effects Model for Semi-Continuous Data (HurdleLogNormal)

> **Note:** `HurdleLogNormal` is not yet implemented in the Python port.
> It will be available in a future release.  In the R package the model is
> defined via a custom family object and fitted as:
>
> ```r
> km1 <- mixed_model(y ~ sex * time, random = ~ 1 | id, data = DF,
>                    family = hurdle.lognormal(), n_phis = 1,
>                    zi_fixed = ~ sex)
>
> # Extend with a random intercept in the zero part (uncorrelated)
> km2 <- update(km1, random = ~ 1 || id, zi_random = ~ 1 | id)
>
> # Marginalised coefficients for (1 - π) × E{log(Y)}
> marginal_coefs(km2)
> ```
>
> The hurdle log-normal family models continuous data with excess zeros.  A
> logistic regression governs whether the response is zero, and a linear mixed
> model with log-normal errors governs the positive part.  The estimated
> dispersion parameter `exp(phis)` gives the standard deviation of the
> log-normal error terms.

## Two-Part / Hurdle Poisson Mixed Effects Model

> **Note:** `HurdlePoisson` is not yet implemented in the Python port.
> It will be available in a future release.  In the R package hurdle Poisson
> and hurdle negative binomial models are fitted as:
>
> ```r
> dm1 <- mixed_model(y ~ sex * time, random = ~ time | id, data = DF,
>                    family = hurdle.poisson(), zi_fixed = ~ sex)
>
> # Extend with a random intercept in the zero part
> dm2 <- update(dm1, zi_random = ~ 1 | id)
>
> anova(dm1, dm2)
> ```
>
> The hurdle Poisson family models count data with excess zeros via a two-part
> model: a logistic regression for the zero / non-zero split and a
> zero-truncated Poisson distribution for the positive counts.  Note that the
> fixed-effects coefficients for the positive counts relate to the mean $\mu$
> of the **full** (untruncated) Poisson distribution — not to the mean
> conditional on being positive, which is $\mu / (1 - e^{-\mu})$.

## Two-Part / Hurdle Negative Binomial Mixed Effects Model

> **Note:** `HurdleNegativeBinomial` is not yet implemented in the Python
> port.  It will be available in a future release.  In the R package:
>
> ```r
> hm1 <- mixed_model(y ~ sex * time, random = ~ time | id, data = DF,
>                    family = hurdle.negative.binomial(), zi_fixed = ~ sex)
>
> # Extend with a random intercept in the zero part
> hm2 <- update(hm1, zi_random = ~ 1 | id)
>
> anova(hm1, hm2)
> ```
>
> The hurdle negative binomial family is identical in structure to the hurdle
> Poisson family but replaces the zero-truncated Poisson with a zero-truncated
> negative binomial distribution, thereby accommodating over-dispersion in the
> positive counts.
